Issued at 1000 PM MDT Fri Oct 30 2026

RAIN SHOWERS FRIDAY NIGHT AND SATURDAY EVENING:

A band of rainfall driven by a transient shortwave is steadily 
moving through the region tonight. Impacts will be minimal, 
though we have seen a stronger embedded thunderstorm or two 
develop, so don't rule out a few stronger outflow gusts. 
Otherwise, rainfall is steady and light. Per CAM's, the line of 
showers will continue northeastwards before departing the CWA 
late Saturday morning, making way for a relatively calm Saturday
afternoon thanks to a "dry" spell. We're using the term "dry" 
very lightly as PWAT's will still be about 150% of normal (give 
or take 50% depending on which ensemble you listen to). This is
enough to produce a few isolated showers across the region, so 
don't be surprised if you see a brief bout of rainfall during 
the afternoon hours. For most of the region though, little more
than cloudy skies is to be expected through 6:00 PM MDT. After 
6:00 PM, the upper-level jet strengthens overhead, which could 
produce a few stronger thunderstorms south of US-50 which may 
bolster a very slight flash flood risk should localized heavily 
rainfall track over vulnerable areas. As things stand now 
though, impacts are expected to be minimal and/or very 
localized.

RAINFALL, SNOWY MOUNTAINS, AND POTENTIAL FLOODING:

A robust Atmospheric River arrives on Sunday bringing well 
above normal amounts of moisture for this time of year across 
the Desert Southwest. Guidance continues to show precipitation
arriving at the Four Corners region Sunday before sunrise and
spreading northeastwards throughout the morning. The ECMWF Ens 
is running wetter than the GFS Ens for this storm with PWAT's 
about 0.1-0.25 inches higher in the former regionwide (and as a 
result, similar margins regarding QPF). So, we do still lack
some confidence on the exact magnitude of precipitation
accumulations. As far as the NBM is indicating though, areas 
along the US-160 corridor east of Cortez have a 50-70% of seeing
2 or more inches of rainfall. At higher elevations in the San 
Juans, QPE is expected to sit over 3 inches in most areas. 
Considering the notable rainfall these same areas experienced 
last week, flooding concerns are back on the table, and a Flood
Watch is in place. More in the Hydrology section below.

We mentioned 3 or more inches of QPE in the San Juans with this
storm system, but much of this water is expected to come down 
as snow as cold air underneath the passing trough moves 
overhead. Temperatures will begin to be more noticeably affected
beginning near mid-afternoon Sunday as high temperatures are 
stunted, reaching only into the low-to-mid 50's for valleys and
the 30's to low-40's for most mountain locations (with some 
areas unlikely surpass freezing during the day). Cold air 
advection will continue throughout the night as well as the 
storm progresses. What this means for precipitation across the 
region is that snow levels will begin relatively high Sunday 
afternoon (around 11,000 feet) before descending over the next 
24-36 hours, likely reaching as low as 7,500 to 8,000 feet. Snow
ratios wouldn't be overly impressive given the anticipated 
temperatures, but given the amount of available moisture we'll 
be experiencing, sufficient factors are in place for well over a
foot of snow in the San Juan mountains. Confidence is low on a 
range of snow accumulations given the transition from rain to 
snow for most areas, but 14-20 inches currently looks like the 
most likely range above 11,000 feet and much more variable 
accumulations below this elevation. In the central Colorado 
mountains, locations above 11,000 feet are in line for 10-15 
inches of snow, meanwhile the Grand Mesa and Flat Tops, 
considering their lower elevations, are facing 6-12 inches. As a
result, Winter Weather highlights are in effect Sunday and 
Monday. In passes, snow may be slushy given the lower snow 
ratios, so be mindful should you be traveling through the 
mountains Sunday or Monday.
